paras: The Canton, Texas, night shootings were a series of attacks in early August 1885 in and near Canton, in Van Zandt County, in which armed white men fired into Black homes at night, wounding Ben Fullbright and killing Bob Prewitt. A coroner's jury attributed Prewitt's death to a resident of Canton, but no arrest was reported, and the Dallas Herald's correspondent described local officials as unable or unwilling to act.

Ben Fullbright, described by the Dallas Herald's Canton correspondent as "one of the leading negroes of the county," lived in the suburbs of Canton and was "said to be very offensive to a large class of white men." The San Antonio Light attributed the trouble to "an obnoxious negro politician," without naming him.

On the night of August 3, a party of some 40 men went to the house of Jim Ross, a Black man, and fired into it several times, shooting out his lamp. Fullbright was in the house and appeared to be the man the party wanted, but he left the premises, and he and others were said to have recognized several of the attackers.

On a later Wednesday night, unknown men came to Fullbright's own house and shot him in the shoulder with twelve buckshot, putting the muzzle of a gun through a crack in the wall. One of the party then shot Bob Prewitt in the back as he stepped into the house, and Prewitt died the following Saturday morning. Around the same time a Black church was burned in the southern part of the county, an item the Herald reported separately and the San Antonio Light joined to the shootings.

A coroner's jury held an inquest over Prewitt's body and returned a verdict that he died of a gunshot wound inflicted by a person living in Canton, whose name the Herald printed as a blank. Fullbright remained in critical condition and said he knew who had shot him. According to the correspondent, the sheriff wanted to bring the guilty to justice but could get no support, since a majority of citizens and some officials thought the slayers deserved sympathy.

One leading citizen offered "a chromo" to the shooter and another said he would give $25 to shake his hand. The county attorney said he was afraid to proceed lest someone "plug him" through his window at night, and no report of an arrest or indictment appears in the coverage.

The fullest account came from the Dallas Herald's Canton correspondent, whose letter dated August 14 ran in the daily Herald on August 15 and in the weekly Herald on August 20. The correspondent wrote that no charges against either man justified "such rash acts" and concluded that it was "easy to imagine how powerless the law is" in the county.

The San Antonio Light, in a column of state news on August 15, reduced the events to a "war of races" in which whites had raided the Black houses of Canton, gave the dead as two, and repeated without comment that a Black politician was said to be the cause.

The San Antonio Light reported two Black men killed, while the Canton correspondent named one dead, Prewitt, and one wounded, Fullbright; the local letter, which names the victims and reports an inquest, is the more detailed source.

reader.title: Canton, Texas, night shootings (1885)
bases: The local correspondent describes two night attacks aimed at one Black man, Ben Fullbright, by a party of some 40 and then by unknown persons, in which Fullbright was wounded and Bob Prewitt killed, along with a church burning elsewhere in the county (A1, A3); the San Antonio brief instead describes a general raid on Black houses (A2).

Two Texas papers with differently worded reports agree that whites attacked Black homes in Canton with gunfire, that Black men were killed and that a Black church was burned in the south of Van Zandt county (A1, A2), though they differ on the number killed and it is not shown that the San Antonio brief is independent of the Canton correspondent.

accounts.label: Canton correspondent of the Dallas Herald
accounts.gist: Two night attacks aimed at Ben Fullbright: a party of some 40 shot into Jim Ross's house, then unknown men shot Fullbright and killed Bob Prewitt; an inquest named a Canton resident, but the sheriff had no support and the county attorney was afraid to act.

accounts.label: San Antonio Light state-news brief
accounts.gist: A 'war of races' in Van Zandt county: whites raided Black houses in Canton, a Black church was burned, an 'obnoxious negro politician' was said to be the cause, and two Black men were killed.

framing.detail: The Dallas Herald correspondent wrote that no charges against either man justified 'such rash acts' and closed that it was 'easy to imagine how powerless the law is', reporting the sympathy of citizens and officials for the slayers.
The San Antonio Light headed nothing but ran the item among state news as a 'war of races' and repeated without comment that an 'obnoxious negro politician' was said to be its cause.

conflicts.note: The Canton correspondent's letter is local and gives names and an inquest, so its count is the better evidence; the San Antonio brief names no source and no victims.
